Well, distress? Absolutely. It’s... it’s a heavy thing to carry around. As for interfering with my life, it’s a bit complicated. I mean, on paper, I’m still functioning. I’m still getting up at 5:00 AM, still making it to the site, still managing my crews, still hitting my deadlines. The job gets done because, well, the job has to get done. I’ve never been one to let the ball drop professionally. 

But outside of work? That’s where the cracks are really starting to show. It’s... it’s embarrassing, honestly. I used to be a pretty active guy socially. I’ve got a group I’ve known for years, and we used to do things. We had this walking club, right? A bunch of us guys would get together on the weekends, walk a few miles, grab a coffee, talk about the market or sports or whatever. And my wife and I used to have a subscription to the local theater, we’d go to shows a couple of times a month. 

But lately... I’ve just been turning all of that down. I’ll make up excuses. I’ll say I’m too tired from the site, or I’ve got paperwork to catch up on, or my knee is acting up. But the truth is, I’m just... I’m so ashamed. I feel like this massive fraud. Well, uncomfortably full? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know what you're getting at, that feeling like you've just eaten Thanksgiving dinner and you have to unbutton your pants and lay on the couch for three hours. But it's not really like that for me. 

Don't get me wrong, I eat a lot during these... these episodes, as you called them. Like I mentioned with the cookies, it's a significant amount of food. But my stomach doesn't usually get to that point of physical pain or stretching where I feel like I'm going to burst. I've always had a pretty cast-iron stomach, to be honest. Even back when I was a young guy working my way up on the framing crews, eating whatever garbage I could grab from the food trucks on a fifteen-minute break, I never really got stomach aches. 

So, yeah, I'm definitely eating way past the point of just being satisfied, and mentally, like I said, I feel absolutely sick about it. I feel heavy with the guilt of it all. But physically? My stomach itself doesn't usually hurt. I don't get that bloated, painful sensation where I'm physically uncomfortable from the sheer volume of it. It's more of a... a mental discomfort, I suppose you could say. The physical feeling of fullness is there, sure, but it doesn't cross over into actual physical pain or extreme discomfort. It's just... it's the lack of control that's the uncomfortable part, not my actual stomach.

Guilt? Oh, absolutely. It’s… it’s overwhelming, to be honest. The guilt and the self-disgust, it just washes over me. It’s funny you ask if it’s during or after, because it’s really both, but they feel different.

The disgust starts building right then. I look at my hands, I look at the food, and I just feel this deep, profound disappointment in myself.

I’ll look at the empty wrappers or the dent I put in the pantry, and I just feel sick to my stomach—not physically, like we talked about, but mentally. I feel like a complete failure. If a subcontractor is slacking, I’m the first one to pull them aside and read them the riot act. But here I am, unable to manage myself. 

I’ll just stand there in the kitchen, and this wave of shame just completely engulfs me. I think about what my crew would say if they saw me. I think about what my wife would think if she really paid attention and saw the sheer volume of what I’m putting away. It’s just… it’s a terrible, terrible feeling. It makes me feel weak. And in my line of work, in my life, weakness isn't something I tolerate well, especially not in myself. So, yeah, the guilt and the disgust… they’re probably the hardest parts of this whole thing. Yeah... yeah, that's exactly it. Compulsion, urge, whatever you want to call it. It’s actually the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and made the appointment to see you. 

What brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can literally see myself doing it and telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. It’s the most bizarre, frustrating thing in the world. Because, you have to understand, my whole life, my entire career, is built on control and precision. If a concrete pour is going sideways on a site, I step in, I blow the whistle, I tell the crew to stop, and everything stops. My brain gives the command, and the action follows. 

But standing there at that kitchen island... it's like the wiring between my brain and my body is completely severed. I’m standing there, looking at the food, and in my head, I am yelling at myself. I'm saying, "Put the package down. Walk away. You don't want this." I am actively, consciously telling myself to stop. But it's like I'm just a passenger in my own body watching a movie of someone else. My hands just keep going back into the pantry, reaching into the box, bringing it to my mouth, over and over again. 

I've worked with my hands my entire life, right? From framing houses back in the day to drafting blueprints, my hands have always done exactly what I told them to do, down to the fraction of an inch. So to stand in my own house, with my wife twenty feet away watching her shows, and just watch my own hands keep grabbing food while my brain is screaming to shut the whole operation down... it's terrifying, frankly. It really is. I just completely lose the ability to steer the ship. That's why I'm sitting here talking to you today. Because I can't manage my own two hands once that switch flips, and I just can't live with that feeling of having absolutely zero choice in the matter.

A need? I... I'm not really sure I'd use that word. I don't know if I've ever noticed it feeling like a *need*, exactly. 

I mean, regular hunger, sure, I know exactly what that feels like. You spend thirty-five years in the construction business, you learn what real, physical hunger is. You're out there on a site in the middle of July, sun beating down on the back of your neck, you've been on your feet since five in the morning, hauling materials, checking grades, arguing with the suppliers... by the time noon rolls around, your stomach is completely hollow. You *need* fuel. Your body is physically demanding calories just to keep the engine running so you don't pass out on the scaffolding. That's a need. You eat because if you don't, you can't work.

But this thing at night? I don't feel hungry. Not in that way. And I don't really feel an intense *need* to eat the food, either. It's not like my brain is screaming at me that I absolutely have to have a sleeve of crackers or a row of cookies. I'm not craving it. I don't have this irresistible desire welling up inside me where I feel like I have to act on it because I just *have* to taste the food or satisfy some deep urge. 

Honestly, I don't really know what to tell you on that front, because I just haven't noticed any kind of 'need' driving the whole operation. Like I was saying a minute ago, it's more of a mechanical failure. I'm just standing there, and my hands are doing the work, but there's no craving or intense emotional need pushing me to do it. It's not a need I'm trying to satisfy. If anything, I'm actively *not* wanting it while it's happening. 

So, no, I can't really say it feels like an irresistible need... I'm not entirely sure what you mean by that, to be honest. I don't feel a drive to do it, I just... do it. Without needing to. Does that make any sense? Because I'll tell you, it doesn't make a lick of sense to me. I just don't feel that specific 'need' you're talking about at all.

I'll eat half a sleeve of cookies, then a bag of pretzels. It just keeps escalating. I end up eating... I mean, it's far, far more than I would ever put on a plate for a normal supper. If you laid it all out on the counter before I started, it would look like I was feeding a whole crew of guys, not just myself. That's... that's really the crux of the whole issue, and honestly, it's what finally pushed me to make this appointment. I mean, I'm a logical guy, right? I spend my days analyzing blueprints, identifying structural flaws, anticipating problems before they happen. I’m still getting up at 5:00 AM, still making it to the site, still managing my crews, still hitting my deadlines. The job gets done because, well, the job has to get done. Autopilot is exactly the word for it. Honestly, like I was telling you a few minutes ago, that specific feeling is exactly what brings me in here to see you. It is completely automatic. \n\nYou know, it’s kind of like... well, if you've ever driven the exact same route to a job site every single morning for six months straight. You leave the house at 4:30 AM, you get on the highway, you take the exit, and suddenly you're pulling your truck into the dirt lot and you don't even remember making the last four turns. Your brain just checked out, but your body did the driving. It’s like that, but honestly, it’s worse. Because when you're driving on autopilot, you're just spacing out. But with this... with the food... I am fully awake. I am completely aware. \n\nI’m standing there at the island, the television is murmuring in the living room—usually my wife is watching one of those home renovation shows, which, don't even get me started on how fake those are, the timelines they show are an absolute joke—and I'm just... operating. Like a piece of heavy machinery that got switched on, but the kill switch is busted. I'm looking at my own hand reaching into the pantry, grabbing whatever it is, bringing it up, chewing, swallowing, and then reaching right back in again. \n\nMy brain is screaming, \"Abort, shut it down, we're done here,\" but the body is just running its own program. I'm totally disconnected from it. So yes, autopilot is exactly it. You're just a passenger. And I've got to tell you, it's the most powerless, frustrating feeling in the world for a guy who has spent his entire adult life being the one in charge, the one steering the ship, making sure everyone else is doing exactly what they're supposed to do. To have my own body just go rogue on me like that... it’s completely out of my hands. Literally.\n\nDoctor: During these nighttime eating episodes, do you ever feel detached from yourself, like you're not fully present or you're watching yourself act from outside your body?\n\nPatient: Yeah, exactly. I mean, it's like I've been trying to explain to you this whole time, right? That specific feeling is the exact reason I'm sitting in this chair today. Like I said, what brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can literally see myself doing it and telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. \n\nWhen you say \"watching yourself act from outside your body,\" that hits the nail right on the head. It's... well, let me put it this way. You know when you're looking at a set of blueprints, and you're looking down at the whole floor plan from above? You can see where the load-bearing walls are, where the HVAC runs, the whole layout. You have this bird's-eye view of the entire operation. That's exactly what it feels like in my kitchen. \n\nI'm standing there by the kitchen island—we just put that granite in two years ago, beautiful stone, absolute nightmare of a subcontractor though, I had to stay on him every single second to make sure the seams lined up right—anyway, I'm standing there at the island, but it's almost like my mind is hovering up near the crown molding, just looking down at this sixty-year-old guy shoving food into his mouth. \n\nI am totally detached. I'm up there, so to speak, shouting down at myself, going, \"Hey! Cut it out! Stop reaching into the cabinet! Put it away!\" But the guy down there—which is me—just keeps doing it. It's the strangest, most unsettling thing. I'm present enough to know it's happening, and I'm actively trying to call off the job, but I'm completely disconnected from the physical act itself. Like my brain and my body are on two completely different job sites. \n\nSo, yeah, detached is a very good word for it. It's just... it's exactly what I was saying before. I see myself doing it, I tell myself to stop, and I just can't. The hands just keep moving, completely on their own, while I just have to stand there and watch it happen from the outside. It's infuriating, doc, it really is. You spend your whole life building things, controlling every little detail on a massive project, and then you can't even control your own hands in your own house.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm that these episodes of uncontrollable eating only happen in the evening or during the night, and not during other parts of the day?\n\nPatient: Well, confirm? I don't know if I can confirm that, doc. I really couldn't say for sure if it's strictly a nighttime operation. I'm honestly not entirely sure. \n\nYou see, in my line of work, the whole concept of 'day' and 'night' gets pretty blurry anyway. You've got jobs where we have to pour concrete at three in the morning because the city won't let us shut down the street during normal traffic hours. Or you're stuck in the site trailer at two in the afternoon on a Tuesday, fighting with the city inspectors over some permit issue that should have been resolved three weeks ago, and you end up working straight through dinner. My schedule is just a complete moving target, always has been. Thirty-five years of it, and you never really get a standard nine-to-five. You're just constantly putting out fires whenever they pop up.\n\nBecause my days are so all over the map like that, my eating habits are kind of all over the map, too. I might be grabbing a quick sandwich from a roach coach at ten in the morning, or I might eat absolutely nothing at all until I finally drag myself through the front door at seven. I just don't know. \n\nI haven't really kept a punch list of the exact times it happens. I just haven't tracked it that closely to give you a solid yes or no on whether it's only happening after dark.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever experience this same feeling of being detached from yourself or watching yourself from outside your body at times other than these nighttime eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Detached at other times? If I spaced out or detached on a job site, somebody could get seriously hurt, or we'd pour a foundation wrong and cost the client hundreds of thousands of dollars. \n\nSo, no, that whole... bird's-eye view thing I was telling you about? It goes against everything I am. But no, to answer your question, I haven't noticed that disconnected feeling anywhere else in my life. Just with the food.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself feeling detached, emotionally numb, or overwhelmed by negative emotions during times other than these nighttime eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying about the detachment... no, not really. You get mad, sure. You get frustrated. I'll be the first to admit I can yell with the best of them when a sub is trying to cut corners. My blood pressure probably spikes, and I definitely bring some of that aggravation home with me. \n\nBut overwhelmed by it? Or numb? No, no, no. You can't be numb in this business. If you go numb, the whole project falls apart. You have to be loud, you have to be completely present, you have to push through it and find a solution. I've been doing this for thirty-five years. I started right out of high school swinging a hammer, framing houses in the dead of winter, and worked my way up to managing these massive commercial sites. You don't survive in this industry by getting overwhelmed and shutting down. You just... you fix the problem. You adjust the schedule, you fire the guy who isn't pulling his weight, you just get it done. \n\nSo no, I don't have any of that numb feeling or whatever you want to call it during my regular day-to-day. I have to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself not remembering these nighttime eating episodes afterward, or do you always remember exactly what happened while you were eating?\n\nPatient: Well, remember it... yeah, I remember it. You know, you'd think so, right? That's exactly what I thought at first. I tried to track it, you know, kind of like trying to find the root cause of a structural failure on a site. I figured, okay, if I can just figure out what the trigger is, I can fix the problem. 

But... no. I really can't pin it on a bad day. I mean, don't get me wrong, my job is basically just managing stress for a living. Every single day there's something. You've got weather delays, you've got a concrete truck showing up two hours late and the mix is already starting to set, or you've got some architect changing the specs on a whim and expecting my guys to just magically make the steel bend to their will. That's just me in my recliner. But during all of that—whether I'm active, whether I'm watching TV, whether I'm brushing my teeth—I am not eating. I'm not raiding the pantry, I'm not sitting there stuffing my face while we're watching Jeopardy. I might have a glass of ice water or maybe a beer, but the urge to just gorge myself? It's completely zero. \n\nIt really is strictly a middle-of-the-night thing. I have to actually go to bed, turn the lamp off, and fall asleep first. It's only later, when I wake up at one or two in the morning, that the switch flips and I head to the kitchen. So yeah, I don't have these episodes before I go to sleep. When I'm awake in the evening, I'm fully in control. It's only after my head hits the pillow that all bets are off."
